No. 26A 
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, APPLICANT
v. 
STATE OF CALIFORNIA, ET AL. 
───────────
APPLICATION FOR INJUNCTION PENDING APPEAL 
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT
AND REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE INJUNCTION
───────────
D. JOHN SAUER
 Solicitor General 
 Counsel of Record 
 Department of Justice 
 Washington, D.C. 20530-0001 
 SupremeCtBriefs@usdoj.gov 
 (202) 514-2217

ii 
PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING
The United States of America is the applicant here and was plaintiff-appellant 
below. The State of California; Shirley Weber, California Secretary of State; and 
Dean Logan, County of Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, are respondents here and were defendants-appellees below. Services, Immigrant Rights and Education Network; Mi Familia En Accion; League of United Latin American Citizens; 
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People; and California-Hawaii 
State Conference of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People 
are also respondents here and were intervenors-appellees below. 
RELATED PROCEEDINGS
United States District Court (C.D. Cal.)
United States v. California, No. 26-cv-12025 (Oct. 28, 2026)
United States Court of Appeals (9th Cir.):
United States v. California, No. 26-7231 (Oct. 30, 2026)
United States v. California, No. 26-7070 (Oct. 26, 2026)

(1) 
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
No. 26A 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, APPLICANT
v. 
STATE OF CALIFORNIA, ET AL. 
───────────
APPLICATION FOR AN INJUNCTION PENDING APPEAL
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT
AND REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE INJUNCTION
───────────
Pursuant to Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. 
1651, the Solicitor General—on behalf of the United States—respectfully requests 
that this Court issue an injunction pending appeal in this case. In addition, because 
the United States’ irreparable injury is ongoing, the United States respectfully requests an administrative injunction pending the Court’s consideration of this application. 
Congress has made it “unlawful for any alien to vote” in any federal election. 
18 U.S.C. 611. Enforcing that exclusion of aliens is “part of the sovereign’s obligation 
‘to preserve the basic conception of a political community.’” Foley v. Connelie, 435 
U.S. 291, 296 (1978). Yet despite that prohibition, aliens sometimes register to vote, 
and do vote, in our elections. That unfortunate reality is evidenced by New Jersey’s 
recent admission that it has thousands of aliens on its voter rolls and that hundreds 
of those aliens have voted. See Matt Friedman, “It’s the honor system,” Politico, July 
30, 2026, https:perma.cc/VN6NE-TK7J. It is also evidenced by California’s past ad-

2 
mission that “a mistake caused as many as 1,500 noncitizens being registered to vote 
in the state.” Mark Osborne, 1,500 noncitizens may have been registered to vote in 
California DMV error, ABC News, Oct. 9, 2018, https://perma.cc/9RM4-THZX.
In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified 
more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based 
on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, 
in the United States’ view, are likely not U.S. citizens. The United States asked the 
district court and the Ninth Circuit for an injunction requiring California to segregate 
mail ballots cast by those persons until the lawfulness of the ballots could be adjudicated. The lower courts denied that relief, with Judge Bumatay dissenting from the 
Ninth Circuit’s decision. This Court should grant the “modest remedy” requested by 
the United States—“stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens.” App., infra, 22a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). “This solution would 
not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.” Ibid.
The United States is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal. The district 
court concluded that the United States lacks Article III standing to bring this suit, 
but the United States suffers a judicially cognizable “injury to its sovereignty” from 
the “violation of its laws,” Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex 
rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765, 771 (2000)—here, the law prohibiting aliens from voting 
in federal elections. The district court also concluded that the United States lacks a 
cause of action, but under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), a litigant (including 
the United States) generally may sue in equity to prevent state action that violates 
federal law. The court of appeals and district court determined that California has 
the power to adopt its own procedures for verifying voter qualifications, but a State’s

3 
procedures cannot control the operation of a federal statute such as Section 611. 
The equities also favor granting an injunction. Once California commingles 
the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots 
back. The only way to preserve the district court’s ability to grant relief to the United 
States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots 
now. That remedy would not cause any undue hardship to California. To the contrary, California’s own election laws contemplate the segregation of challenged ballots, and the segregation of challenged ballots is a standard remedy in election cases. 
To be sure, California and the United States disagree about the likely unlawfulness of the ballots at issue. “These dueling allegations can and should be investigated.” App., infra, 130a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). In the meantime, however, an 
interim injunction is necessary “to preserve the relative positions of the parties until 
a trial on the merits can be held.” University of Texas v. Camenisch, 451 U.S. 390, 
395 (1981). To that end, the Court should issue a “limited injunction directing California to stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones” pending completion of the United States’ appeal to the Ninth Circuit and further review in this Court. 
App., infra, 36a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). 
STATEMENT
Congress has made it “unlawful for any alien to vote in any election” for President, Senator, or member of the House of Representatives. 18 U.S.C. 611(a). The 
Executive Branch uses a multi-step review process to identify aliens who may have 
violated that prohibition. See C.A. Doc. 28, at 17-20 (Oct. 29, 2026). First, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reviews state voter rolls with the help of 
Accurint, a third-party data analytics and investigative platform that can use a 
voter’s name and address to find additional data, such as his social security number,

4 
birth date, and phone number. See id. at 17-18. After USCIS removes those whom 
it can identify as U.S. citizens, investigators from the Fraud Detection and National 
Security Directorate (a component of USCIS) manually review the remaining names. 
See id. at 19. Homeland Security Investigations (a component of U.S. Customs and 
Immigration Enforcement) conducts a further review before referring individuals for 
potential criminal investigation. See id. at 19-20. 
As this Office has been informed, after processing a publicly accessible version 
of California’s voter roll ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Executive Branch 
identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered as voters in California at the time the voter-roll information was received and whom the United 
States believes are likely to be aliens. See C.A. Doc. 28, at 20. On October 13, 2026, 
the federal government delivered a list of those individuals to the California Secretary of State and the Los Angeles County Registrar. See ibid. But the state officials
have declined to cooperate with the United States by sharing the full unredacted version of its current voter roll. See ibid. 
On October 15, the United States sued in the United States District Court for 
the Central District of California. App., infra, 46a. It named the State of California, 
the California Secretary of State, and the Los Angeles County Registrar as defendants. Ibid. Several civil-rights organizations intervened. Ibid. On October 19, relying on Section 611, the United States asked the district court to issue an order directing California to segregate—not to cancel—any mail ballots cast by the challenged 
individuals until those individuals’ citizenship could be verified. Id. at 46a-47a.* 
On October 22, before the district court acted on the United States’ motion, the 
* California law generally requires mail ballots to be postmarked by Election 
Day and to be received by seven days after Election Day. See Cal. Elec. Code § 3020(b).

5 
United States appealed to the Ninth Circuit and sought an injunction pending appeal. 
App., infra, 71a. The Ninth Circuit denied the motion and dismissed the appeal for 
lack of appellate jurisdiction, rejecting the contention that the district court’s inaction 
had amounted to a constructive denial of the United States’ request for relief. Id. at 
66a-82a. Judge Bennett issued a concurring opinion concluding that the United 
States’ claim also fails on the merits. Id. at 83a-107a. Judge Sanchez issued a concurring opinion concluding that Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 (2006) (per curiam), 
precludes relief at this stage. App., infra, 108a-121a. Judge Bumatay issued a dissenting opinion concluding that the court of appeals had jurisdiction and that the 
United States is entitled to relief. Id. at 122a-156a. 
On October 28, the district court denied the relief requested by the United 
States. App., infra, 40a-65a. The court determined that the United States does not 
have standing or a cause of action to bring this claim, id. at 48a-52a; that the United 
States is unlikely to succeed on its claim that Section 611 preempts California’s actions, id. at 52a-56a; that the relief sought by the United States would likely violate 
other federal election laws, id. at 56a-59a; and that the equities did not support granting relief, id. at 59a-65a. 
The Ninth Circuit denied the United States’ motion for an injunction pending 
appeal. App., infra, 1a-21a. The Ninth Circuit first determined that it had appellate 
jurisdiction because the district court’s order, though labeled as the denial of a temporary restraining order, was “tantamount to a denial of a preliminary injunction.” 
Id. at 7a; see id. at 4a-7a. The Ninth Circuit also assumed that the United States 
has Article III standing and a cause of action to enforce Section 611. Id. at 4a. But 
it then concluded that the United States is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its asapplied claim that Section 611 preempts California’s actions to count the ballots of

6 
suspected noncitizens, id. at 8a-14a; that the relief sought could violate other federal 
statutes, id. at 14a-16a; that the United States does not face irreparable harm, id. at 
17a-18a; and that granting relief at this stage would contravene Purcell, id. at 18a21a. Judge Bumatay issued a dissenting opinion concluding that the court of appeals 
should have granted the United States’ “reasonable request” to segregate “likely 
noncitizen ballots” until their lawfulness could be adjudicated. Id. at 39a; see id. at 
22a-39a. 
ARGUMENT
Under Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. 1651, 
the Court may grant an injunction pending the disposition of an appeal. See Libby v. 
Fecteau, 145 S. Ct. 1378, 1378 (2025). Under the familiar standard for an interim 
injunction, the applicant must show that it is likely to succeed on the merits, that it 
faces irreparable harm, and that the balance of hardships and public interest favor 
interim relief. See Winter v. NRDC, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). As usual when considering an application for interim relief, this Court also considers whether the underlying case warrants the Court’s review. See Does 1-3 v. Mills, 142 S. Ct. 17, 18 
(2021) (Barrett, J., concurring in the denial of application for injunctive relief). A 
request for an injunction usually requires a “higher justification than a request for a 
stay because, unlike a stay, an injunction does not simply suspend judicial alteration 
of the status quo but grants judicial intervention that has been withheld by lower 
courts.” Respect Maine PAC v. McKee, 562 U.S. 996, 996 (2010). 
Those general principles are subject to “refinement” in “the election context.” 
Merrill v. Milligan, 142 S. Ct. 879, 881 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in grant of 
applications for stays). In that context, the proper interim remedy when a litigant 
brings a potentially meritorious challenge to the validity of a ballot is generally to

7 
segregate the ballot until its lawfulness can be adjudicated. See, e.g., Roe v. Alabama 
by and through Evans, 43 F.3d 574, 583 (11th Cir. 1985). “Count first, and rule upon 
legality afterwards, is not a recipe for producing election results that have the public 
acceptance democratic stability requires.” Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections, 
607 U.S. 71, 80 (2026). Indeed, here, it would be too late to ascertain the lawfulness 
of suspected unlawful ballots after they have been commingled with lawful ballots. 
The issuance of interim relief in Republican Party of Pennsylvania v. Boockvar, 
2020 WL 6536912 (Nov. 6, 2020), illustrates those principles. There, the Pennsylvania General Assembly had set a deadline of 8 p.m. on election day for receiving mail 
ballots, but the Pennsylvania Supreme Court had extended that deadline by three 
days. See Republican Party of Pennsylvania v. DeGraffenreid, 592 U.S. 1287, 1288
(2021) (Thomas, J., dissenting from the denial of certiorari). Justice Alito, as Circuit 
Justice, ordered that “all ballots received by mail after [the deadline set by the state 
legislature] be segregated” from other ballots and that “all such ballots, if counted, be 
counted separately.” Boockvar, 2020 WL 6536912, at *1. Fortunately, the segregated 
ballots ultimately did not affect the outcome. See DeGraffenreid, 592 U.S. at 1290 
(Thomas, J., dissenting from the denial of certiorari). 
Under that standard, this Court should issue an interim injunction directing 
California to segregate ballots cast by the individuals who may be registered to vote 
in California and have been identified by the federal government as likely noncitizens. That “modest remedy” “would not cancel any vote”; instead, it would just “sto[p] 
California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens” and would 
“allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.” App., infra, 22a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). Each of traditional factors supports that “reasonable request.” 
Ibid.

8 
A. The United States Is Likely To Succeed On Appeal
Federal law provides that it “shall be unlawful for any alien to vote in any 
election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of 
President, Vice President, Presidential elector, Member of the Senate, [or] Member 
of the House of Representatives.” 18 U.S.C. 611(a). An alien may vote only if “the 
election is held partly for some other purpose,” “aliens are authorized to vote for such 
other purpose” under state law, and “voting for such other purpose is conducted independently of voting for a candidate for [a] Federal office.” Ibid. A violation is a 
crime, punishable by up to a year of imprisonment. See 18 U.S.C. 611(b). 
Because it is “unlawful for any alien to vote” in a federal election, 18 U.S.C. 
611, it follows that any ballot cast by an alien is unlawful. It also follows that a State 
may not count such an invalid ballot. After all, a State must give “full value and 
effect” to votes cast by qualified U.S. citizens. United States v. Saylor, 322 U.S. 385, 
386 (1944). Valid votes may not be “impaired, lessened, diminished, [or] diluted.” 
Ibid. Just as a State may not debase or dilute valid votes by stuffing a ballot box with 
fictitious votes, see Ex parte Siebold, 100 U.S. 371 (1879), it also may not debase or 
dilute valid votes by tabulating invalid votes. 
In this case, this Office is informed that the Executive Branch has identified 
over 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on 
publicly accessible information and who, based on the Executive Branch’s review, are 
likely not U.S. citizens. Those individuals have received mail ballots, consistent with 
state law requiring that every registered voter be sent such a ballot. See Cal. Elec. 
Code § 3000.5. Yet California is now poised to tabulate ballots cast by those individuals. If it turns out that those individuals cast ballots but are not, in fact, U.S. citizens, then California’s counting of their votes will violate Section 611 and will debase

9 
or dilute valid votes cast by U.S. citizens. 
The litigants, to be sure, dispute whether the individuals identified by the 
United States are registered voters in California who are actually aliens. But to obtain interim relief, the United States need not show that it will definitely prevail at 
the conclusion of the litigation. For now, a likelihood of success is enough, and the 
United States has shown a sufficient likelihood that California is about to violate the
law by counting aliens’ ballots. That likelihood supports an interim injunction requiring California to segregate the questioned ballots until their lawfulness can be 
adjudicated. 
The court of appeals and district court identified several reasons for rejecting 
that conclusion. None is meritorious. 
Standing. The district court (though not the court of appeals) first concluded 
that the United States lacks Article III standing. See App., infra, 48a-51a. That 
theory is wrong because the United States has Article III standing to enforce its own 
laws. See id. at 133a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). In general, every sovereign has a 
judicially cognizable “sovereign interes[t]” in its “power to create and enforce a legal 
code, both civil and criminal,” “within the relevant jurisdiction.” Alfred L. Snapp & 
Son, Inc. v. Puerto Rico ex rel. Barez, 458 U.S. 592, 601 (1982). More specifically, the 
Executive Branch—which has the power to “execut[e]” the laws, U.S. Const. Art. II, 
§ 1, Cl. 1, and the duty to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” U.S. Const. 
Art. II, § 3—has a judicially cognizable sovereign interest in enforcing federal statutes. It is therefore “beyond doubt” that the United States suffers a judicially cognizable “injury to its sovereignty” from any “violation of its laws.” Vermont Agency of 
Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765, 771 (2000); see, e.g., 
Stauffer v. Brooks Brothers, Inc., 619 F.3d 132, 1325 (Fed. Cir. 2010) (“The parties

10
have not cited any case in which the government has been denied standing to enforce 
its own law.”); United States v. Yarbrough, 452 Fed. Appx. 186, 189 (3d Cir. 2011) 
(rejecting as “frivolous” the contention that the United States lacked “standing to enforce its own laws”). 
The district court insisted that the United States has not suffered an Article 
III injury because the United States retains the ability to indict and prosecute aliens 
who cast ballots in California. See App., infra, 49a. The United States’ argument in 
this case, however, is that federal law not only prohibits aliens from voting in federal 
elections but also prohibits California from counting their illegal votes. The United 
States suffers just as much an Article III injury from a violation of the latter requirement as it does from a violation of the former one. To be sure, California might contest the United States’ reading of Section 611; it might believe that, although Section 
611 bars aliens from voting, it leaves California free to count the aliens’ illegal votes. 
But any such argument goes to the merits, not standing. In general, “standing in no 
way depends on the merits of the plaintiff’s contention that particular conduct is illegal.” Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490, 500 (1975); see, e.g., FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate, 596 U.S. 289, 298 (2022). 
Cause of action. The district court (but not the court of appeals) also concluded that the United States lacks a cause of action. See App., infra, 51a-52a. That, 
too, is incorrect. See id. at 137a-138a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). Generally, a plaintiff 
may sue in federal court for equitable relief “against state officers who are violating, 
or planning to violate, federal law.” Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center, Inc., 575 
U.S. 320, 326 (2015); see, e.g., Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123, 150-151 (1908). Such 
suits for equitable relief may be brought not only by private plaintiffs, but also by the 
United States. See, e.g., Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012); United States

11
v. South Carolina, 720 F.3d 518 (4th Cir. 2013); see also 3 Joseph Story, Commentaries on the Constitution of the United States § 1668 (1833) (“It would be a perfect 
novelty in the history of national jurisprudence, as well as of public law, that a sovereign had no authority to sue in his own courts. * * * A sovereign without the means 
of enforcing civil rights, or compelling the performance, either civilly or criminally, of 
public duties[,] * * * would be a most extraordinary anomaly.”). 
Instead of focusing on Ex parte Young (the case that governs suits in equity 
against state actors), the district court focused on In re Debs, 158 U.S. 564 (1895) (a 
case addressing suits in equity against private parties). App., infra, 51a-52a. The 
court reasoned that Debs allows the federal government to “sue in equity without a 
statutory grant of authority” only “to protect ‘a property interest’” or to prevent an
“‘interference with national security or a burden on interstate commerce.’” Id. at 51a. 
Because this suit is brought against state actors rather than private parties, however, 
this suit may proceed even assuming for the sake of argument that the district court 
is right about the scope of Debs. A private party could invoke Ex parte Young to 
challenge a State’s violation of federal law, even if that violation does not impair a 
property interest, interfere with national security, or burden interstate commerce. 
The United States may avail itself of the same equitable right of action as such a 
private party. 
Preemption. The court of appeals and district court both concluded that the 
United States is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its claim that federal law 
preempts California’s counting of the challenged ballots. App., infra, 8a-14a, 52a56a. Section 611, however, unambiguously provides that “[i]t shall be unlawful for 
any alien to vote in any [federal] election.” 18 U.S.C. 611(a). A state law or practice 
that allows an alien to vote in a federal election, or that treats an alien’s vote as valid,

12
conflicts with that provision and so is preempted. See App., infra, 30a-33a.
The court of appeals emphasized that the Elections Clause provides that “[t]he 
Times, Places and Manners of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, 
shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof.” U.S. Const. Art. I, § 4, 
Cl. 1; see App., infra, 8a-9a. As the court recognized, however, the Elections Clause 
also provides that “Congress may at any time make or alter such Regulations.” U.S. 
Const. Art. I, § 4, Cl. 1. Further, under the Supremacy Clause, a state election law—
like any other state law—is subordinate to laws enacted by Congress pursuant to its 
other enumerated powers. See U.S. Const. Art. VI, Cl. 2. The fact that the Elections 
Clause authorizes California to regulate elections thus does not advance the analysis; 
if a California election regulation conflicts with Section 611, it must yield. 
The court of appeals also found it “unclear (at best) whether Congress intended 
§ 611 to have any preemptive effect, much less a preemptive effect that forces states 
to set aside their own state election laws and procedures.” App., infra, 12a. But a 
federal law’s preemptive effect does not flow from Congress’s “intent” that the law 
have such an effect. Instead, it flows directly from the Supremacy Clause, which 
provides that “the Laws of the United States” are “the supreme Law of the Land,” 
“any Thing in the * * * Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding.” U.S. 
Const. Art. VI, § 2. Section 611, by virtue of the Supremacy Clause, preempts any 
conflicting state law or action; no further showing of congressional “intent” is required. 
The court of appeals observed that California has its own ban on voting by 
aliens and that California enforces that ban by requiring applicants to attest to their 
citizenship under penalty of perjury. App., infra, 11a. But that misses the point. 
California is entitled to prescribe the procedures it deems appropriate for enforcing

13
its own state-law ban on alien voting, but those state procedures do not control the 
operation of Section 611’s separate federal ban on alien voting. In general, when
applying federal law, “a federal court must make an independent inquiry, whether or 
not there has been an inquiry by [state officials], and irrespective of how any such 
inquiry may have turned out.” Elkins v. United States, 364 U.S. 206, 224 (1960). 
For example, if the United States were to bring a criminal prosecution against 
an individual for violating Section 611, a federal court obviously would not be bound 
by California’s procedures for determining the individual’s citizenship. California’s 
acceptance of the individual’s attestation might be relevant evidence, but it would not 
be conclusive. A civil suit to enforce Section 611 should work the same way. If the 
United States shows in such a civil suit that a particular individual is in fact an alien, 
then a federal court should order the State to refrain from counting that person’s 
ballot—whatever effect that individual’s contrary attestation might have for purposes 
of state law. Similarly, if the United States establishes at a preliminary stage that 
there is a likelihood that an individual is in fact an alien, then a federal court should 
order that the person’s ballot be segregated until the factual dispute can be resolved—
again, whatever effect that individual’s attestation might have under state law. 
Other federal laws. The court of appeals and district court both concluded that 
the segregation of ballots would likely violate the National Voter Registration Act of 
1993 (NVRA), and the district court concluded that it would also likely violate the 
Voting Rights Act Amendments of 1970 (Voting Rights Act) and the Civil Rights Act 
of 1964 (Civil Rights Act). App., infra, 15a-16a, 56a-59a. Those conclusions all lack 
merit. See App., infra, 38a-39a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). 
The NVRA provides that a State may not conduct, within the 90 days before 
the date of a federal election, “any program the purpose of which is to systematically

14
remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.” 52 
U.S.C. 20507(c)(2)(A). This Court will consider, later this Term, whether that provision restricts a State’s ability to remove aliens from the voter rolls. See RNC v. Mi 
Familia Vota, No. 25-1017 (oral argument scheduled for Dec. 8, 2026). But even assuming the provision does so, the provision would not preclude the relief here. The 
relief sought by the United States would require only that ballots be segregated—not 
that anyone be removed from the official list of eligible voters. The court of appeals 
speculated that “the consequence” of such relief might ultimately be “the removal of 
voters” found to be ineligible, App., infra, 15a, but the NVRA’s text focuses on “the 
purpose” of the program, not its predicted consequences, 52 U.S.C. 20507(c)(2)(A). 
See 26-7070 C.A. Doc. 32, at 12 (Oct. 24, 2026) (Los Angeles County Registrar’s acknowledgment that “this lawsuit is not about maintenance of voter rolls”). 
The Voting Rights Act provides that “[n]o person acting under color of law shall 
fail or refuse to permit any person to vote who is * * * qualified to vote, or willfully 
fail or refuse to tabulate, count, and report such person’s vote.” 52 U.S.C. 10307(a). 
But aliens are not “qualified to vote.” And segregating a person’s ballot until his 
citizenship can be confirmed does not amount to a “fail[ure] or refus[al]” “to permit 
[the] person to vote” or “to tabulate, count, and report such person’s vote.” Ibid. The 
segregation of the ballot simply defers a decision on whether to tabulate, count, and 
report the vote until the vote’s validity can be ascertained. 
Finally, the Civil Rights Act provides that “[n]o person acting under color of 
law shall in determining whether any individual is qualified under State law or laws
to vote in any election apply any standard, practice, or procedure different from the 
standards, practices, or procedures applied under such law or laws to other individuals within the same county, parish, or similar political subdivision who have been

15
found by State officials to be qualified to vote.” 52 U.S.C. 10101(a)(2)(A). There are 
multiple reasons why that provision is beside the point here, but the simplest is that 
it is limited to “determin[ations] whether any individual is qualified under State law 
or laws to vote.” Ibid. (emphasis added). This case concerns whether individuals are 
qualified under a federal statute, see 18 U.S.C. 611(a), not under state law. 
Facts. The central factual issue in this case is whether the individuals identified by the federal government are registered voters in California who are casting 
ballots and are, in fact, aliens. The district court suggested (albeit in addressing the 
equities rather than the merits) that the federal government’s allegations “are not 
credible.” App., infra, 60a. But that conclusion is legally erroneous. 
To begin, the United States has not yet had a full opportunity to prove its 
claims. The United States’ witnesses were available to testify at the district court’s 
hearing. See C.A. Doc. 28, at 33. Yet the court declined to hear their testimony and 
instead chose to resolve the case on the papers. See ibid. In these circumstances, the 
court’s conclusions concerning the credibility of the United States’ allegations carry 
little weight. 
Regardless, the district court committed clear error in rejecting the United 
States’ factual contentions. The United States has submitted declarations explaining 
what data it used to match registered voters to noncitizen records. See C.A. Doc. 28, 
at 33-34; D. Ct. Doc. 22-3 (Oct. 19, 2026); D. Ct. Doc. 22-4 (Oct. 19, 2026). The district 
court raised a series of objections to the United States’ evidence, but it identified no 
affirmative evidence on the other side. In other words, the United States has identified numerous individuals who are, in its view, likely aliens, but the district court did 
not point to any evidence that any of those individuals is actually a citizen. 
In all events, this Court need not resolve any factual disputes about whether

16
any particular individual is a California voter and is an alien or a citizen. The sole 
issue for now is whether California should be required to segregate the challenged 
ballots until such factual disputes can be resolved by the lower courts in the first 
instance. The United States has made a sufficient showing to justify granting that 
relief. 
B. The Other Factors Support Injunctive Relief
To obtain an interim injunction, the United States must also show that the 
underlying case warrants this Court’s review, that it faces irreparable harm, and that 
the balance of hardships and public interest tip in its favor. Those factors support 
granting this application. 
Certworthiness. The United States has a profound interest in the integrity of 
federal elections. See Burroughs v. United States, 290 U.S. 534, 545 (1934); Ex parte 
Yarbrough, 110 U.S. 651, 657-658 (1884). More specifically, the United States has a 
profound interest in ensuring that aliens do not participate in those elections. “It is 
fundamental to the definition of our national political community that foreign citizens 
do not have a constitutional right to participate in, and thus may be excluded from, 
activities of democratic self-government.” Bluman v. FEC, 800 F. Supp. 2d 281, 288 
(D.D.C. 2011) (three-judge court) (Kavanaugh, J.). Congress has sought to pursue 
that interest by prohibiting aliens from voting in federal elections. See 18 U.S.C. 611. 
That vital national interest is undermined by allowing aliens to vote, and to have 
their votes counted, in the face of evidence that their ballots are unlawful. A decision 
of the Ninth Circuit sustaining a procedure leading to such an outcome would warrant this Court’s review. 
Irreparable harm. The United States faces irreparable harm in the absence 
of injunctive relief. “California admits that there is no way to trace a ballot after it

17
is processed.” App., infra, 149a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). “So there is no way for the 
district court to repair the government’s injury”—“noncitizens voting in a federal 
election”—“after a full merits proceeding.” Ibid. Put another way, “[i]naction means 
that suspected noncitizens’ votes are forever commingled and the federal government 
loses out on any possible redress.” Id. at 130a. That injury “grows every day,” “as 
hundreds of thousands of ballots” arrive and are counted. Id. at 149a. That injury 
will continue to mount through Tuesday, November 10 (a week after election day, 
California’s deadline for receiving mail ballots). See p. 4 n.*. That injury can be 
prevented by a “limited injunction preventing California election officials from mixing 
the ballots of those identified as suspected aliens * * * with the rest of the ballots.” 
App., infra, 148a-149a. 
The court of appeals determined that the United States was unlikely to suffer 
irreparable harm because its “preemption argument is likely unavailing” and because 
the district court “found that the United States’s process in creating the [list] was not 
credible.” App., infra, 17a. But those arguments assume that the United States is 
wrong on the merits and thus make the irreparable-harm inquiry redundant with the 
likelihood-of-success inquiry. The relevant question in granting interim relief is instead whether, “assuming the applicant’s position on the merits is correct, there [is] 
a likelihood of irreparable harm” if interim relief is not granted. Philip Morris USA 
Inc. v. Scott, 561 U.S. 1301, 1301 (2010) (Scalia, J., in chambers) (emphasis added); 
see Barnes v. E-Systems, Inc. Group Hospital Medical & Surgical Insurance Plan, 
501 U.S. 1301, 1302 (1991) (Scalia, J., in chambers) (“There must be * * * a likelihood 
of irreparable harm (assuming the correctness of the applicant’s position).”). If the 
United States is correct, and the individuals it has identified (or even some of those 
individuals) turn out to be aliens who are unlawfully voting in California, then the

18
United States will suffer irreparable harm from the commingling of their ballots with 
lawful votes.
Balance of hardships and public interest. The court of appeals and district 
court credited California’s representations that the interim relief sought by the 
United States would “provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of 
the election.” App., infra, 18a. That doomsday prediction ignores that segregating 
ballots is a routine remedy when the lawfulness of ballots is questioned. California
law itself contemplates the segregation of challenged ballots, providing that “challenged ballot[s] shall be set aside” and that “[r]esolution of challenged ballots shall 
take place in a segregated area * * * to avoid confusion and mixing of ballots.” Cal. 
Code Regs. Tit. 2, § 20363. Moreover, one county registrar has attested that “locating 
and segregating challenged ballots is entirely possible.” App., infra, 37a-38a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). Following the segregation procedure that California’s own law 
already establishes may prove to be “a challenge,” “[b]ut difficulty is no reason for 
courts to throw [their] hands in the air and give up—not when the threat is illegal 
votes undermining our elections.” Id. at 37a. 
The court of appeals and district court invoked Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 
(2006) (per curiam), which establishes that, as a general matter, federal courts should 
not alter state election rules on the eve of an election. But that principle does not 
apply here. See App., infra, 153a-155a (Bumatay, J., doctrine). Purcell limits federal 
judicial intervention in the period before votes are cast. This case, however, concerns 
what happens after votes are cast. It is well established that, at that point, federal 
courts may issue appropriate relief to enforce federal law, see, e.g., Bush v. Gore, 531 
U.S. 98 (2000) (per curiam)—including by requiring the segregation of challenged 
ballots until their lawfulness can be determined, see Boockvar, 2020 WL 6536912.

19
That distinction between pre-voting and post-voting intervention makes sense. 
Purcell rests chiefly on the understanding that voters need to know “the rules of the 
road” (“how, when, and where” to vote), DNC v. Wisconsin State Legislature, 592 U.S. 
1039, 1043 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring), and that “[c]ourt orders affecting elections” can “result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from 
the polls,” Purcell, 549 U.S. at 4-5. It also reflects the recognition that “[l]ate judicial 
tinkering with election laws can lead * * * to unanticipated and unfair consequences 
for candidates, political parties, and voters.” Merrill, 142 S. Ct. at 881 (Kavanaugh, 
J., concurring in grant of applications for stays). Those concerns simply do not arise 
after voting has already occurred. Here, “whether state officials commingle ballots 
that have already been submitted can’t possibly cause voter confusion about how, 
when, or where to vote—the only ballots affected will already have been cast.” App., 
infra, 153a-154a (Bumatay, J., dissenting). Nor does segregating ballots threaten
unfair consequences for candidates, political parties, or voters. Instead, it “just gives 
election officials a chance to determine whether ballots are legal.” Id. at 154a. 
CONCLUSION
This Court should issue an injunction, pending the United States’ appeal to 
the Ninth Circuit and any subsequent proceedings in this Court, that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified 
as likely noncitizens. The Court should also enter an administrative injunction to 
that effect while it considers this application.
Respectfully submitted.
